newsitem.title: USA: IMF dollar rhetoric underscores G-7 policy dilemma.
newsitem.headline: IMF dollar rhetoric underscores G-7 policy dilemma.

text.p: The IMF voiced only modest concern with dollar strength on Wednesday, calling exchange rates "reasonably consistent" with fundamentals and underscoring the dilemma that policymakers from wealthy nations face in curbing the greenback's rise.
Until economic fundamentals shift and become less dollar-supportive, currency experts believe Group of Seven finance officials have their hands tied.

Michael Mussa, economic counsellor and director of research at the IMF, told a briefing on Wednesday that an expected slowdown in the U.S. economy later this year could ultimately pressure the dollar.
But before any such fundamental turnaround takes place, analysts said the prospects of active G7 intervention to rein in the dollar remain slim.

"If the circumstances arose in which there seemed to be a market reassessment of the fundamentals, intervention couldn't be ruled out, but under the current circumstances I would guess it to be a long shot," said John Lipsky, chief economist at Chase Manhattan Bank.
Among the G7 nations, Japan has been the most vocal in their opposition to further yen weakness and corresponding dollar strength.
The weakening of the yen has sapped investor confidence in Japan's asset markets and underscored the shaky status of its economy.
Japanese officials have repeatedly warned of intervention to halt the yen's slide in recent weeks and called currency market fluctuations out of line with fundamentals.
And in the wake of such rhetoric, foreign exchange traders have been on edge, fearing more tough talk at a meeting of G7 finance officials this weekend.
But on Wednesday, the IMF's Mussa seemed to play down the sense of urgency expressed by Japanese officials and the need for any near-term action to curb the dollar.

He said that further depreciation of the yen, particularly against the dollar, would not be welcome, but also conceded that such an outcome would not be a source of "extreme nervousness or intense concern."

Mussa's remarks echoed commentary in the IMF's World Economic Outlook, released on Wednesday, which said that the appreciation of the U.S. dollar had been supported by the continued strong performance of the U.S. economy and by associated interest differentials.
"The IMF is saying that the currency movements we've had are reflective of the cyclical positions of the major economies," said Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities in New York.
Analysts said the market believes the U.S. and Japan both want to put a stop to the dollar's rise, but recognize that ultimately they will need help from the economic fundamentals.
As a result, BZW's Iggo said he expected this weekend's G7 meeting to produce the same subdued statements on exchange rates that were seen at the last G7 meeting in February in Berlin.
Policymakers at the February meeting said that major currency misalignments noted in an April 1995 communique had been corrected and that currency stability was desirable.
